statement: Marks on a number line are equally spaced. The 1st mark is labelled 4 and the 3rd mark is labelled 10. What number is at the 6th mark?

choices.misconception: I started at the 3rd mark, 10, and counted on 1 for each mark after it: 11, 12, 13.
I thought the 1st to the 3rd mark is 3 steps, so I shared 6 into 3 steps of 2.
I stopped at the 5th mark instead of the 6th.
I thought there were 6 steps from the 1st mark to the 6th mark, so I added 3 six times to 4.

hints: Count the gaps between marks, not the marks.
From the 1st mark to the 3rd mark there are only 2 gaps. Find how much one gap is worth, then count gaps from a mark you know.
The jump from 4 to 10 is 6, shared over 2 gaps, so each gap is 3. Now count on from 10 to the 6th mark.

solutions.reliable: From the 1st mark to the 3rd mark is 2 gaps, and from 4 to 10 is 6, so each gap is 3. The marks are 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, 19, so the 6th mark is 19. The idea to keep: on a number line, count gaps, not marks.
solutions.elegant: From the 3rd mark to the 6th mark is 3 gaps of 3, so add 9 to 10: 19.

whyOnTest: Gaps versus marks is the fence-post idea on a number line, and it decides almost every scale-reading problem.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
